content: "Continuing in the tradition of 19th-century thought, some still cling to the notion that ‘great men’—those uniquely gifted, bold, and charismatic individuals—single-handedly shape the course of history through sheer force of personality and brilliance. This idea, popularized by Scottish philosopher Thomas Carlyle, positions figures like Aristotle, Julius Caesar, Napoleon, Martin Luther, and Prophet Muhammad as heroic titans whose actions fundamentally and permanently altered the world. According to Carlyle, the masses were passive onlookers, destined only to admire, applaud, and obediently follow these exceptional leaders. Despite the rise of more inclusive and egalitarian historical theories—including Marxist interpretations and E.P. Thompson’s ‘history from below’—the myth of the heroic leader endures. In the modern era, however, this romanticized view has become increasingly problematic. While the allure of such hero-worship persists, many who see themselves as today’s ‘great men’ are not noble saviors but rather anti-heroes or outright villains. Often men driven by hubris, they believe they possess a divine or historical mandate to rule, lead, or ‘save’ nations through authoritarian means. They claim exclusive insight and a sacred duty, imposing their will ruthlessly and often destructively on others. This mindset, still influential in politics and culture, elevates arrogance and power over empathy and collaboration. Ultimately, the essay argues that the myth of the ‘great man’ not only oversimplifies history, but also poses a dangerous misconception—equating power and ambition with heroism, when all too often such figures leave behind legacies of turmoil, oppression, and violence instead of progress and justice."
